titleEn: Laws of Hammurabi — §141–152: runaway wives, sick wives, and debts in marriage (xxiii 33 – xxv 60)
part: Laws §141–152 · bad wives, sick wives & debts in marriage (Col. xxiii 33 – xxv 60)
about: Twelve laws on marriages in trouble. A wife who plays the fool, wastes her house and belittles her husband is convicted; if he divorces her she gets nothing for her journey or her divorce payment, and if he does not, he may take a second woman while she stays on in his house as a servant (§141). A woman who rejects her husband has her case examined: if she is blameless she takes her dowry and goes home, and if not she is thrown into the water (§142–143). Then the slave-woman and the šugītum, two women beside the wife: a husband whose wife gave him a slave-woman who bore sons may not take a šugītum (§144); a husband whose wife bore him no sons may (§145), but the šugītum does not rank with the wife; a slave-woman who bears sons and then rivals her mistress cannot be sold, though the mistress may mark her as a slave, and if she bore none the mistress may sell her (§146–147). A husband whose wife falls ill may take another woman but may not divorce the sick one (§148); if she will not stay, she leaves with her dowry (§149). A wife given property by deed passes it to the son she loves (§150). Last, debts: a husband’s earlier debts cannot be collected from his wife, nor a wife’s earlier debts from her husband, but a debt made during the marriage is paid by both (§151–152). Harper’s transliteration writes the Sumerian signs for ‘woman’, ‘house’, ‘silver’, ‘merchant’ and ‘slave-woman’ as Akkadian words, and each of them was read from the plate; the few doubtful spellings are marked in the notes.

sentences.l: If the-wife of-a-man who in the-house of-a-man is-living to going-out her-face has-set-and, a-folly she-plays-the-fool,
sentences.i: If a man’s wife, who is living in a man’s house, has set her face to go out, and plays the fool,
sentences.n: A new law, and it opens with a long “if”: read it as a chain of clauses. šumma begins it, aššat awīlim is “the wife of a man” (aššat is aššatum in the construct state, “wife of”, with awīlim in the genitive), and ša ina bīt awīlim wašbat is a relative clause, “who is living in a man’s house” (wašbat, “she dwells”, is the stative of wašābum, as in §130). ana wuṣîm is ana + infinitive, “to go out”: the first sign is PI, which reads wa or wu, and the infinitive of waṣûm is wuṣûm. panīša ištakan, “she has set her face”, is the idiom for making up one’s mind (iškun “he set” in the perfect, with -ta- after the first sign: ištakan); -ma ties it to the next clause. zikiltam izakkil sets a noun beside a verb of the same root, “she plays the fool’s part”: Harper’s glossary files the two words under šikiltu “the part of a fool” and šakālu “to play the part of a fool” (his text spells them with z, and the lemmas here follow the signs); that is his sense, and the pair is UNCERTAIN by later standards. The wife’s misconduct goes on into the next unit.

sentences.l: her-house she-neglects, her-husband she-belittles, they-shall-convict-her-and,
sentences.i: she neglects her house and belittles her husband — they shall convict her, and
sentences.n: More of her conduct, then the verdict begins. bīssa is bītum “house” + -ša “her”: the t and the š meet and are said ss, and the plate writes the house-sign É followed by the sign ZA (Harper’s bî-za). uzappaḫ is the D-stem of sapāḫum “to scatter”, here “to neglect” (Harper: “to scatter, to neglect”), present tense. mussa is mutum “husband” + -ša “her”, written mu-za (the spelling used throughout §127–140), and ušamṭa is the Š-stem of maṭûm “to be small”, “to make small, belittle” (Harper: “to make little, to belittle”), present tense like uzappaḫ: the present of a Š-stem of a verb ending in a vowel ends in -â, the preterite in -i, and the signs spell -a. Harper prints the sign DA as da; the verb needs it read ṭa. The exact vowel is UNCERTAIN. ukannūšima is the D-stem of kânum “to be firm” — “to prove against, convict” — with -ši “her” and -ma “and”: this is the start of the apodosis, and the sentence goes on.

sentences.l: If her-husband I-divorce-her (?) has-said, he-shall-divorce-her; her-journey (?), her-divorce-payment, anything not will-be-given-to-her.
sentences.i: If her husband has said, “I divorce her,” he shall divorce her; nothing shall be given to her for her journey (?) or her divorce payment.
sentences.n: A divorce by the husband’s word, with the word quoted. ezibša is what he says: ezēbum “to leave, to divorce” + -ša “her”. Harper prints e-ṣi-ib-ša; the sign is ZI and is read zi here, as in izzibši and īzibšim. The form itself is UNCERTAIN: the object “her” on a verb is normally -ši, so -ša is unexpected; the quoted sense “I divorce her” is fixed by the clause that follows. iqtabi is the perfect of qabûm “to say” and closes the quotation; the code’s “says” is a perfect, “has said”. izzibši, “he shall divorce her”, is the present of ezēbum with -ši “her”. ḫarrānša and uzubbûša are two payments she does not get: uzubbûm is “divorce payment” (a rare word, Harper’s reading), and ḫarrānum is Harper’s “way, road, journey, errand”, so ḫarrānša “her journey” is a guess at a travel-allowance (UNCERTAIN); Harper’s own translation takes it as “on her departure”. mimma ul innaddiššim is “nothing shall be given to her”: innaddin is the N-stem (passive) of nadānum “to give”, and the n of the stem is swallowed before -šim “to her” (the signs iš-ši-im).

sentences.l: If her-husband not I-divorce-her has-said, her-husband a-woman another he-shall-take,
sentences.i: If her husband has not said, “I divorce her,” her husband may take another woman,
sentences.n: The opposite case: lā ezibša iqtabi is the same quotation with lā “not”. zinništam šanītam is “another woman”: zinništum “woman” is written with the single sign SAL, the very sign that spells aššatum “wife” (§128): only the context tells which; šanītam is the feminine accusative of šanûm “other, second”. iḫḫaz is the present of aḫāzum “to take”, “he shall take”. The code has no word for “may”: a permission is the plain present tense, and the English “may” follows the sense, which is settled by the contrast with ul iḫḫaz “he shall not take” in §144.

sentences.l: woman that like a-slave-woman in the-house of-her-husband she-shall-live.
sentences.i: and that woman shall live in her husband’s house like a slave-woman.
sentences.n: Her place in the house. kīma amtim is “like a slave-woman”: kīma “like, as” takes the genitive; amtum “slave-woman” is the Sumerogram GEME₂, the signs SAL and KUR, with no ending written (Harper prints amtim). The plate shows the two signs and no ending after them. ina bīt mutiša uššab is “in her husband’s house she shall live”: mutiša is “her husband”, uššab the present of wašābum “to dwell” — the verb of wašbat in the first law. The woman of the “if”, the wife who has behaved badly, is not divorced here: zinništum šī is her, and she stays in the house as a slave-woman in rank, while the second woman (§141, šanītam) becomes the wife.

sentences.l: If a-woman her-husband she-hated-and, not you-will-take-me she-has-said,
sentences.i: If a woman hates her husband and says, “You shall not take me,”
sentences.n: §142, the woman who refuses her husband. izīrma is zêrum “to hate” in the preterite (izīr, long ī, with -ma “and”). Then she speaks: ul taḫḫazanni is “you shall not take me (as wife)”, the same verb as iḫḫaz in the last law (aḫāzum, present 2nd person, ta-), with -anni “me” (the ventive -am + -ni), and iqtabi “she has said” closes the quotation. mussa, here the object, is written mu-za as before.

sentences.l: her-case in her-babtum it-shall-be-decided-and,
sentences.i: her case shall be decided in her babtum (?),
sentences.n: The court’s step. warkassa is warkatum “the circumstances, the facts of the case” + -ša, “her case” (the t and š said ss, as in bīssa). ipparras is the N-stem (passive) of parāsum “to decide”, present: “it shall be decided”, with -ma “and”. babtiša is babtum + -ša, and babtum is UNCERTAIN: Harper glosses it “loss, defects”; in §126 it was the accused party (“the one blamed”), and later dictionaries read it as a city quarter or ward. Here it may be “as to her faults” (Harper) or “in her quarter”; the translation leaves the word and the question open.

sentences.l: if she-is-careful-and a-fault not she-has,
sentences.i: if she has been careful and has no fault,
sentences.n: Two conditions, each a short clause. naṣratma is the stative of naṣārum “to watch, guard”; of a person, “she is circumspect, she takes care” (Harper), with -ma “and”. ḫiṭītam is a reading to check: Harper prints ḫi-di-tam, but the middle sign is DI, which also reads ṭi, so the word is ḫiṭītum “sin, fault” with lā īšu “she does not have” (īšu is išûm “to have”, 3rd person, read as a present). Harper’s glossary does not list the word, so the identification is UNCERTAIN.

sentences.l: and her-husband he-goes-out-and greatly he-belittles-her,
sentences.i: and her husband goes out and about (?) and greatly belittles her,
sentences.n: More of the husband. u is “and”, written with the sign Ù. waṣīma is Harper’s wa-zi-ma: the verb waṣûm “to go out” (his glossary lists the form under that verb), spelled with the sign ZI read ṣi: “he is going out”; the nuance is not written, and “out and about” (a husband who neglects her) is UNCERTAIN. magal “greatly”. ušamṭaši is ušamṭa as in §141 plus -ši “her”, “he belittles her” (Harper’s u-ša-am-da-ši, with DA read ṭa). Harper prints mu-za(g): his (g) marks a sign with strokes added to its usual form (as in ni-ši(g) in the prologue); here it is read as the ZA sign, UNCERTAIN.

sentences.l: woman that guilt not she-has; her-dowry she-shall-take-and to the-house of-her-father she-shall-go.
sentences.i: that woman has no guilt: she shall take her dowry and go to her father’s house.
sentences.n: The verdict. zinništum šī arnam ul īšu is “that woman — guilt she has not”: arnum is “guilt, offence, penalty”, ul īšu “she has not”; šī “she, that one” is the pronoun in the nominative. šeriqtaša is her dowry (§138); ileqqīma is leqûm “to take” in the present with -ma (Harper’s i-li-qi-ma has the KI sign read qi₂); ana bīt abiša ittallak is “to her father’s house she shall go”, ittallak is the Gt-stem present of alākum “to go” (the Gt gives the sense of going off), the code’s form for “she shall go away”; it is not the Gtn, whose present would be ittanallak. This unit crosses from the last line of column XXIII into column XXIV.

sentences.l: If not she-is-careful-and she-goes-out, her-house she-neglects, her-husband she-belittles,
sentences.i: If she has not been careful, but goes out and about (?), neglects her house and belittles her husband,
sentences.n: §143 is the same facts as §142 with the opposite character. lā naṣratma “she is not careful”; waṣiat is the stative 3rd feminine of waṣûm “to go out” (Harper’s wa-zi-a-at, the ZI sign read ṣi), “she is going out”, and its nuance is UNCERTAIN as before. bīssa uzappaḫ, mussa ušamṭa are the §141 words. The “house” is written bi-za here: the first sign is BI, not the house-sign É that §141 has; it is the same word, bīssa.

sentences.l: woman that into the-water they-shall-throw-her.
sentences.i: they shall throw that woman into the water.
sentences.n: The verdict is the water. zinništam šuāti is “that woman” (šuāti “that, the aforesaid”, accusative); ana mê is “into the water” (mû “water” has the plural form mê); inaddûši is the present plural of nadûm “to throw” + -ši “her”: “they shall throw her”, with the impersonal “they”, as in §129. The punishment is the drowning of the adulteress, set here for a wife who ruins her household.

sentences.l: If a-man a-wife he-took-and, wife that a-slave-woman to her-husband she-gave-and, sons she-caused-to-exist,
sentences.i: If a man has taken a wife, and that wife has given a slave-woman to her husband, and she (the slave-woman) has produced sons,
sentences.n: §144, a new kind of law. aššatam iḫuzma is “he has taken a wife” (iḫuz the preterite of aḫāzum, + -ma); aššatum šī is “that wife”, the SAL sign. amtam is “slave-woman” in the accusative, GEME₂. ana mutiša iddinma is “she gave (her) to her husband”: iddin the preterite of nadānum “to give”, mutiša “her husband”. mārī uštabši is “she has brought sons into being”: mārī is the plural of mārum “son”, the sign TUR with the plural marks ME and EŠ (written DUMU{meš}), and uštabši is the Š-stem perfect of bašûm “to exist”, as in §42: “he has produced”. The subject is not written; the sense is the slave-woman, who has borne the husband’s sons at his wife’s wish. The wife’s gift of a slave-woman is a known marriage arrangement.

sentences.l: man that to a-šugītum taking his-face he-has-set,
sentences.i: and that man has set his face to take a šugītum,
sentences.n: awīlum šū is “that man”, šū being “he, that”. ana šugītim aḫāzim is “to take a šugītum”: ana + the infinitive aḫāzim, which takes its object in the genitive. The šugītum is written {šal}šu-gi₄-tim, the sign SAL as a silent determinative “woman” and then šu-gi₄-tim (Harper prints šu-ge-tim); her exact status is UNCERTAIN, a class of woman set beside the ordinary wife (§137). panīšu ištakan, “he has set his face”, is the idiom of §141.

sentences.l: man that not they-shall-agree-to-him; a-šugītum not he-shall-take.
sentences.i: they shall not agree to that man: he shall not take a šugītum.
sentences.n: The ruling is a refusal, said twice. awīlam šuāti is “that man” in the accusative; ul imaggarūšu is the present plural of magārum “to agree, consent” + -šu “him”: “they will not consent to him”, the “they” being the court, unnamed. Then the same prohibition in the code’s plain form: šugītam ul iḫḫaz, “a šugītum he shall not take”. ul with the present tense is the code’s “shall not”.

sentences.l: If a-man a-wife he-took-and, sons not she-caused-him-to-have-and, to a-šugītum taking his-face he-has-set,
sentences.i: If a man has taken a wife and she has not provided him with sons, and he has set his face to take a šugītum,
sentences.n: §145, the childless wife. The opening is as §144: šumma awīlum aššatam iḫuzma. mārī lā ušaršīšuma is Harper’s u-šar-ši-šu-ma: rašûm “to get, acquire” in the Š-stem is “to cause (someone) to acquire”, with two objects: ušarši + -šu “him” + -ma, “she has not made him acquire sons” (the same verb is in §137: ušaršušu). The exact vowels of the ending are UNCERTAIN. The rest of the “if” repeats §144.

sentences.l: man that a-šugītum he-shall-take; to his-house he-shall-bring-her-in.
sentences.i: that man may take a šugītum and bring her into his house.
sentences.n: Here the permission is given: awīlum šū šugītam iḫḫaz is “that man may take a šugītum” — iḫḫaz, the plain present, used as a permission. ušērribši is the Š-stem of erēbum “to enter”, “to make enter, bring in”, with -ši “her”: “he shall bring her in”. ana bītišu, “into his house”, is written with the house-sign É and the sign šu (Harper’s bîti-šu), no ti.

sentences.l: šugītum that with the-wife not she-shall-make-herself-equal.
sentences.i: That šugītum shall not make herself equal to the wife.
sentences.n: Her rank. šugītum šī is “that šugītum”, nominative (the sign TUM). itti aššatim is “with the wife”: itti “with”, aššatim the wife in the genitive, spelled SAL with tim. ul uštamaḫḫar is the Št-stem of maḫārum “to face, be level with” (Harper’s glossary: III,2, “to take precedence of”), a form that returns in §146 as uštatamḫir. “Make herself equal” is built from the grammar (the Št-stem is reflexive) and matches uštatamḫir in §146; the exact nuance of this verb is UNCERTAIN.

sentences.l: If a-man a-wife he-took-and, a-slave-woman to her-husband she-gave-and, sons she-bore,
sentences.i: If a man has taken a wife, and she has given a slave-woman to her husband, and she (the slave-woman) has borne sons,
sentences.n: §146 starts as §144 but this time the slave-woman has borne sons. ittalad is the perfect of walādum “to bear”, “she has borne” (it-ta-la-ad: the -ta- of the perfect after the first sign); mārī is “sons”, DUMU with MEŠ. The other words are as in §144: aššatam iḫuzma, amtam, ana mutiša iddinma.

sentences.l: afterwards slave-woman that with her-mistress she-has-made-herself-equal,
sentences.i: and afterwards that slave-woman has made herself equal to her mistress,
sentences.n: warkānum is “afterwards”, then amtum šī, “that slave-woman”: GEME₂, the signs SAL and KUR, with no ending written. itti bēltiša is “with her mistress”: bēltum “lady, mistress” (be-el-ti-ša, bēlt + -ša). uštatamḫir is the Št-stem perfect of maḫārum (“to face, be level with”), “she has made herself equal”; compare ul uštamaḫḫar in §145. Harper’s sense (“to take precedence of”) differs, and the nuance is UNCERTAIN.

sentences.l: because sons she-bore, her-mistress for silver not she-shall-give-her;
sentences.i: because she has borne sons, her mistress shall not sell her for silver;
sentences.n: The ruling for the slave-woman: aššum mārī ūldu is “because she has borne sons”: aššum introduces the reason; ūldu is Harper’s ul-du, the preterite of walādum with the subjunctive -u, and its vowels are UNCERTAIN. bēlissa is Harper’s be-li-za: bēlit “mistress” (the construct) + -ša, the t and š said ss, “her mistress”. ana kaspim “for silver” is written with the two Sumerian signs KÙ.BABBAR (kaspum, silver), with no ending. ul inaddišši is nadānum “to give” + -ši “her”: “she shall not give her (for silver)”, that is, sell her; the double š is the stem’s n swallowed (inaddin + -ši).

sentences.l: the-slave-mark (?) she-shall-set-on-her-and, with the-slave-women they-shall-count-her.
sentences.i: she may put the mark of slavery on her, and they shall count her with the slave-women.
sentences.n: What the mistress may still do. abbuttam išakkanšima is “she may set the abbuttum on her, and”: abbuttum is Harper’s “service, slavery” (later dictionaries: the mark of slavery); šakānum “to set, impose”, present, with -ši “her” and -ma. itti amâti imannûši is “they shall count her with the slave-women”: amâti is GEME₂ with the plural mark (the plate shows the SAL-KUR group and further signs; the exact signs of the plural are UNCERTAIN) and imannûši is the present plural of manûm “to count” (“they”, impersonal) + -ši. The present of išakkan reads as a permission, as in §145.

sentences.l: If sons not she-bore, her-mistress for silver she-shall-give-her.
sentences.i: If she has not borne sons, her mistress may sell her for silver.
sentences.n: §147, the other case in a single clause. lā ūlid is “she did not bear” (ūlid, the preterite). Then the words of the last law without ul: bēlissa ana kaspim inaddišši, “her mistress shall give her for silver”, that is, she may sell her; the plain present is again a permission, and the contrast with ul inaddišši in §146 is the whole law.

sentences.l: If a-man a-wife he-took-and, a-sickness has-seized-her,
sentences.i: If a man has taken a wife and a sickness (laʾbum) has seized her,
sentences.n: §148, the sick wife. aššatam iḫuzma as before; Harper prints šuma for šumma on the plate line, which is a misprint (the signs are šum-ma). laʾbum is Harper’s la-ʾa-bu-um, which he glosses “fever, disease”: what the illness is, is UNCERTAIN, and the translation says “a sickness”. iṣṣabassi is the perfect of ṣabātum “to seize” + -ši “her”: the t of the perfect and the š of -ši meet and are said ss, “it has seized her” (the same verb is in §151).

sentences.l: to another taking his-face he-has-set, he-shall-take,
sentences.i: and he has set his face to take another woman, he may take her;
sentences.n: ana šanītim aḫāzim panīšu ištakan is the phrase of §144 with šanītim “another (woman)” in place of šugītim: “to take another”. iḫḫaz is the main verb, “he shall take”, again a permission in the present tense: the husband may remarry.

sentences.l: his-wife whom the-sickness has-seized not he-shall-divorce-her,
sentences.i: but his wife, whom the sickness has seized, he shall not divorce;
sentences.n: aššassu is aššatum + -šu, “his wife” (aš-ša-zu, said aššassu). ša laʾbum iṣbatu is “whom the sickness has seized”: iṣbatu is the preterite of ṣabātum with the subjunctive -u after ša. ul izzibši is “he shall not divorce her” — the same word izzibši as in §141, the verb of divorce.

sentences.l: in the-house he-built she-shall-live-and as-long-as she-lives he-shall-keep-carrying-her.
sentences.i: she shall live in the house that he built, and he shall support her as long as she lives.
sentences.n: The sick wife stays. ina bītim īpušu is “in the house (which) he built”: īpušu is epēšum “to do, make” in the preterite with the subjunctive -u (no ša written), and bītim is the genitive of bītum, written with the house-sign alone. uššabma is Harper’s uš-ša-am-ma: the verb is wašābum, “she shall live” (uššab) with -ma, and the b becomes m before the m of -ma, so it is said uššamma. adi baltat is “as long as she lives”: adi “until, as long as”, baltat the stative of balāṭum “to live”, ba-al-ṭa-at with the DA sign read ṭa. ittanaššiši is the Gtn present of našûm “to carry”, “he shall keep carrying (supporting) her”, with -ši “her”.

sentences.l: If woman that in the-house of-her-husband to-live not she-has-agreed,
sentences.i: If that woman has not agreed to live in her husband’s house,
sentences.n: §149, the sick wife’s choice. zinništum šī is “that woman”, the wife of §148. wašābam is the infinitive of wašābum “to live” in the accusative, and lā imtagar is the perfect of magārum “to agree” (imtagar, with the -ta-; the same verb as imtagarma in §57), “she has not agreed”: she does not want to stay in his house.

sentences.l: her-dowry which from the-house of-her-father she-brought he-shall-make-good-to-her-and she-shall-go.
sentences.i: he shall make good to her her dowry, which she brought from her father’s house, and she shall go away.
sentences.n: The consequence. šeriqtaša ša ištu bīt abiša ublam is “her dowry which she brought from her father’s house”: ublam is the preterite of wabālum “to bring, carry” with the ventive -am, and ištu “from, since”. ušallamšimma is the D-stem of šalāmum “to be whole”, “to make good, restore”, + -šim “to her” + -ma; Harper prints u-ša-lam-šim-ma without a hyphen between ši and im, but the plate shows two signs. ittallak is “she shall go away” (§142).

sentences.l: If a-man to his-wife a-field, an-orchard, a-house and goods he-has-given-her, a-sealed-document he-has-left-her,
sentences.i: If a man has given his wife a field, an orchard, a house and goods, and has left her a sealed document,
sentences.n: §150, a gift to a wife. išrukšim is šarākum “to give as a gift” in the preterite with -šim “to her” (Harper prints iš-ru-uq-šim with q; the sign IG is read uk here, and the root is šarākum, not šarāqum “to steal”). The four gifts are eqlam, kirâm, bītam, bīšam: eqlam is A.ŠÀ (eqlum “field”), kirâm is the sign for “tree” (GIŠ) with the sign for “garden”, read KIRI₆ (kirûm “orchard”), bītam is the house-sign É, and bīšam “goods, property” is written in syllables, bi-ša-am. The plate shows the logograms alone, without endings. kunukkam is “a sealed document”; īzibšim is the preterite of ezēbum “to leave” + -šim, “he left to her” — the deed that makes the gift binding. The last sign of kunukkam is the lozenge KAM (as in našpakam, §120), not KA.

sentences.l: after her-husband her-sons not they-shall-claim-against-her,
sentences.i: after her husband, her sons shall not make a claim against her;
sentences.n: warki mutiša is “after her husband”, meaning after he is gone (his death is not written). mārūša is “her sons”, the subject: DUMU with the plural marks and the sign ša. ul ibaqqarūši is “they shall not claim against her”: baqārum “to claim” (Harper: BAKARU “to make claim”), present plural + -ši “her”; Harper prints i-ba-ga-ru-ši, and the GA sign is read qa₂.

sentences.l: the-mother her-estate to her-son whom she-loves she-shall-give;
sentences.i: the mother shall give her estate to the son she loves;
sentences.n: ummum is “the mother”, nominative. warkassa is warkatum + -ša, as “her case” in §142; here it is “her estate”, what she leaves behind: the sense is UNCERTAIN, since warkatum means “the circumstances, the matter” and “estate” rests on the context. ana mārīša ša irammu is “to her son whom she loves”: DUMU written alone with the sign ša, and irammu, râmum “to love” in the present with the subjunctive -u after ša. inaddin is nadānum “to give”: “she shall give”.

sentences.l: to another not she-shall-give.
sentences.i: to another she shall not give it.
sentences.n: ana aḫim ul inaddin is “to another she shall not give”: aḫûm is “outside, other” (a person outside the family), the phrase ul inaddin the negation of the last unit’s inaddin. Harper reads aḫim as aḫum “brother” (“but to a brother she may not”); “another, an outsider” is the reading used here, and the choice is UNCERTAIN. The mother has freedom among her children; the gift goes to one of the sons, not outside.

sentences.l: If a-woman who in the-house of-a-man is-living so-that the-owner-of-the-debt of her-husband not seizing-her, her-husband she-has-bound, a-tablet she-has-had-left,
sentences.i: If a woman who is living in a man’s house, so that her husband’s creditor may not seize her, has made a contract with her husband and has had a tablet left (as a record),
sentences.n: §151, a husband’s debts. aššum bēl ḫubullim ša mutiša lā ṣabātiša is “so that the owner of the debt of her husband may not seize her”: bēl ḫubullim is the creditor (“owner of the debt”), aššum with a clause gives the purpose, and ṣabātiša is the infinitive of ṣabātum + -ša “her”, with lā “not”: the grammar of the whole phrase is UNCERTAIN. mussa urtakkis is the perfect (D, with -ta-) of rakāsum “to bind”: “she has made a contract with her husband” (Harper’s glossary: “to contract with”). ṭuppam uštēzib is ṭuppum “tablet” (dup-pa-am) + the Š-stem perfect of ezēbum “to leave”, “she has had a tablet left (as a record)”. On this reading the woman is the subject of both verbs; the husband could be the subject of urtakkis, and that is UNCERTAIN.

sentences.l: If that man before woman that he-takes, a-debt upon-him is,
sentences.i: if that man, before he took that woman, had a debt upon him,
sentences.n: lāma is “before” (la-ma) with a verb in the subjunctive: lāma zinništam šuāti iḫḫazu, “before he took that woman”. awīlum šū is “that man”. ḫubullum elišu ibašši is “a debt is upon him”: eli “upon” + -šu, ibašši the present of bašûm “to exist, be there”.

sentences.l: the-owner-of-his-debt his-wife not they-shall-seize.
sentences.i: his creditor shall not seize his wife.
sentences.n: bēl ḫubullišu is “the owner of his debt”, his creditor; the verb iṣabbatū is a plural (-ū), though the subject is written once, so the bēl may stand for the creditors (UNCERTAIN). ul iṣabbatū “he/they shall not seize”; aššassu “his wife”, written aš-ša-zu and said aššassu, as in §148.

sentences.l: And if woman that before into the-house of-a-man she-enters, a-debt upon-her is,
sentences.i: And if that woman, before she entered the man’s house, had a debt upon her,
sentences.n: The mirror-image protasis, opened by u šumma “and if”. lāma ana bīt awīlim irrubu is “before she enters the man’s house”: irrubu is erēbum “to enter” in the present with the subjunctive -u (Harper’s i-ir-ru-bu). ḫubullum elīša ibašši is the same phrase as in the last unit with eliša “upon her”.

sentences.l: the-owner-of-her-debt her-husband not they-shall-seize.
sentences.i: her creditor shall not seize her husband.
sentences.n: bēl ḫubulliša mussa ul iṣabbatu: “the owner of her debt — her husband — they shall not seize”. mussa is “her husband”, here the object, written mu-za; ul iṣabbatū as in the last law. A debt that comes into a marriage with one spouse stays with that spouse.

sentences.l: If after woman that into the-house of-a-man she-entered, upon-them-both a-debt has-come-about,
sentences.i: If, after that woman entered the man’s house, a debt has arisen against both of them,
sentences.n: §152, a debt contracted in the marriage. šumma ištu is “if, after”, and the clause is zinništum šī ana bīt awīlim īrubu, “that woman entered the man’s house” (īrubu is the preterite of erēbum with the subjunctive -u, i-ru-bu). elišunu is eli + -šunu “upon them”, both spouses. ḫubullum ittabši is “a debt has come about”: ittabši is the N-stem perfect of bašûm “to exist”, as in §120: “it has come about”.

sentences.l: both-of-them the-merchant they-shall-pay.
sentences.i: both of them shall pay the merchant.
sentences.n: kilallašunu is Harper’s ki-la-la-šu-nu: kilallān “both” + -šunu “of them”, “both of them”. tamkāram is “the merchant”, the creditor, accusative: DAM.GÀR, the two Sumerian signs (Harper prints it as a single word without hyphens; the plate row is longer than the signs of tamkāram and ippalū alone, so a complement is possible, UNCERTAIN). ippalū is the present plural of apālum “to pay” (Harper’s i-ip-pa-lu): “they shall pay”. The debt is theirs together, and the creditor can be paid by both. This is the last law of the part; §153 follows.
